{"answer": "# Industry AI research disclosure, 2018–2026

**The main change is selective disclosure, not a uniform end to publishing.** In the late 2010s, influential industry papers could arrive with reusable code and pretrained models, as Google’s BERT did. By the mid-2020s, leading labs still published research, but increasingly separated a paper or safety report from access to the system it described: a flagship might be available only through an API, while a different or smaller model was released with downloadable weights. Meta’s Llama family is an important counterexample to a blanket shift toward closed weights, although downloadable weights do not necessarily include training code or data. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041)

## Publication output: what has—and has not—declined

A study of generative-AI research at selected institutions found **some broad decline in publicly available publications from 2023 to 2024, particularly at Google DeepMind**. Across its *January 2020–March 2025* window, fractional-authorship-adjusted totals were 969 papers for Google DeepMind, 64 for Meta, 64 for OpenAI, and 62 for Anthropic. These are totals for a defined generative-AI corpus—not each lab’s complete output, annual counts, or evidence of a continuous decline since 2018. The authors supplemented OpenAlex with OpenAI and Anthropic website publications and warn that Meta may be undercounted. Their annual plot identifies DeepMind’s especially large 2023–2024 fall; it does **not** establish that all four companies followed the same trajectory. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008)

Other measures capture different phenomena. In Stanford’s *2025 AI Index*, industry-only papers among the **100 most-cited AI publications** numbered 17 in 2021, 19 in 2022, and 7 in 2023; that is a decline in this highly cited subset, **not** a count of all industry papers. Conversely, industry originated **55 notable models, or 90.2% of the notable-model set, in 2024**. Academia produced **84.9% of AI publications globally in 2023**. Taken together, these findings show a divergence between who publishes most papers and who develops most notable models; they do not justify saying that industry research or its total publication output fell throughout 2018–2026. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000059)

## How release practices diverged

| Lab | Documented progression | What the progression means |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI** | GPT-2’s full 1.5-billion-parameter model was initially withheld in 2019 and released after smaller models—a staged release. The 2020 GPT-3 paper described a 175-billion-parameter model and its training and evaluation, but the frontier model was not released as downloadable weights. In 2023, the GPT-4 *technical report* expressly omitted model size, architecture details, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, and fuller training methods, citing competition and safety. By the 2025 Transparency Index, its assessed flagship **o3** was an API release. OpenAI also released the separate, smaller **gpt-oss** open-weight models in 2025: its policy was not uniformly closed. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000051) | Publication, API availability, and weight release became distinct decisions. GPT-4 demonstrates that even a substantial public report can withhold information needed to reconstruct training. (pqac-00000041) |
| **Google / Google DeepMind** | Google’s BERT paper, first circulated in 2018, explicitly linked **code and pretrained models**. DeepMind’s 2021 AlphaFold paper made **source code, trained weights, and an inference script** available. Google DeepMind’s 2024 Gemma report released **2B and 7B pretrained and instruction-tuned checkpoints plus open-source inference/serving code**, while its later assessed flagship **Gemini 2.5** was API-accessed. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033) | This is a mixed portfolio, not abandonment of open scientific artifacts: accessible models and code coexist with a closed-weight flagship and the measured 2023–2024 publication decline. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033) |
| **Meta** | The first LLaMA models were described in a 2023 paper but distributed initially to approved researchers under a non-commercial research arrangement. **Llama 2** followed in 2023 with pretrained and chat-tuned releases under conditions permitting commercial use. In 2024 Meta publicly released pretrained and post-trained **Llama 3.1 405B** weights under its Community License, while saying multimodal extensions were *not yet* broadly released. The 2025 Index classified **Llama 4** as open-weight. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000033) | Access widened substantially relative to the initial gate, but release remained selective and licensed. A comparative openness assessment lists Llama 4’s weights as public under restrictions while its training data and training code remained private. (pqac-00000038) |
| **Anthropic** | Anthropic publicly described its **Constitutional AI** training method in a 2022 paper. Yet the **Claude 4** flagship assessed in the 2025 Index was an **API** release, not a public-weight release. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) | Publishing alignment methods and describing a deployed model do not grant researchers its trained parameters or full training pipeline. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) |

Here, *code release* means software is shared; *open weights* means trained parameters can be downloaded and examined or run subject to their license; *full training reproducibility* also requires such inputs as training data, preprocessing, training code and compute information. An API permits experiments on model behavior, but not inspection or local rerunning of its parameters. Neither a paper nor an open-weight download, on its own, establishes that the original training run can be reproduced. The distinction matters particularly for Llama and Gemma: a comparative assessment found publicly available inference code and restricted-license weights for Llama 4 and Gemma 3, but private training data and training code for both. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000038)

## What the Foundation Model Transparency Index measures

The **Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI)** measures disclosed information about companies and their selected flagship models across upstream development, model properties and downstream deployment; it is **not a publication-count index or a simple open-weights ranking**. Its reported mean score was **37/100 in 2023, 58/100 in 2024, and 40.69/100 in 2025**. For the four companies, the directly reported **2024 → 2025** scores were **Anthropic 51 → 46; Google 47 → 41; Meta 60 → 31; and OpenAI 49 → 35**. Thus Meta and OpenAI fell sharply on this measure, while Anthropic and Google fell more modestly. Meta and OpenAI, first and second among the six firms assessed in every edition in 2023, ranked last and second-to-last among those six in 2025. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000035)

The 2025 Index scored **13 developers on 100 indicators**. Only **seven** submitted their own reports; the researchers assembled public-information reports for six others, including Anthropic. Indicators and the company sample changed, some scoring standards became stricter, and the 2024 and 2025 reporting arrangements differed. Consequently, the change in the *overall mean* is not a like-for-like estimate of how much every firm reduced disclosure; individual changes are informative but also need those methodological qualifications. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035)

The Index pinpoints why a model announcement can be scientifically thin: its 2025 **training-data-properties** indicators averaged just **15%**, with eight companies scoring zero on that subdomain. Training compute and post-deployment usage and impact were also poorly disclosed. Developers often reported capability and risk evaluations without enough methods for external reproduction, and the Index found inadequate disclosure of overlap between training material and evaluation sets. Its stricter 2025 reproducibility criterion required shared evaluation **code and prompts**. These are information deficits even when a lab publishes a system card or offers model access. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034)

## Consequences for academic research and reproducibility

Restricted weights and undisclosed data limit the questions an outside laboratory can answer. Researchers can test a permitted API’s outputs, but cannot directly inspect its parameters, independently fine-tune or rerun it locally, reconstruct its data selection, or fully check benchmark contamination and training claims. Access and compute also affect participation: an observational study of **104,226 scientific papers from 2018–2025** associated industry cloud credits with greater reliance on closed/API models, whereas public funding was associated with greater open-weight use. The study does **not** establish that credits *caused* the difference; it instead documents an access-and-control divide that can persist even when academic authors publish their own code. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000034)

There is an important countertrend. An analysis of **56,800 papers** at five AI conferences found that the share documenting **both open code and open datasets** rose from **11% in 2014 to 64% in 2024**; open-code reporting alone rose from 13% to 69%. Its estimated rise in reproducibility from 28% to 64% was **inferred from documentation and earlier replication rates, not established by rerunning every paper**. The study also found no systematic academia-versus-industry documentation advantage across its comparisons. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is **improving openness for published conference experiments alongside persistent—and in some flagship cases worsening—opacity of the most consequential proprietary systems**. Neither trend cancels the other. (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000035)

**Bottom line:** By 2026, industry disclosure had become more *layered and lab-specific*: papers, model cards, safety evaluations, API access, inference code, downloadable weights and training resources could be released separately, at different times, to different users. Evidence supports a notable 2023–2024 fall in Google DeepMind’s measured public generative-AI papers and declining FMTI scores for several flagship developers, but it also documents major open-weight and code releases and improving code/data sharing across AI conference research. A claim that *all* of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and Anthropic simply stopped publishing or opening models between 2018 and 2026 would overstate the evidence. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000055)"}

{"answer": "# Industry AI research disclosure, 2018–2026

**The main change is selective disclosure, not a uniform end to publishing.** In the late 2010s, influential industry papers could arrive with reusable code and pretrained models, as Google’s BERT did. By the mid-2020s, leading labs still published research, but increasingly separated a paper or safety report from access to the system it described: a flagship might be available only through an API, while a different or smaller model was released with downloadable weights. Meta’s Llama family is an important counterexample to a blanket shift toward closed weights, although downloadable weights do not necessarily include training code or data. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041)

## Publication output: what has—and has not—declined

A study of generative-AI research at selected institutions found **some broad decline in publicly available publications from 2023 to 2024, particularly at Google DeepMind**. Across its *January 2020–March 2025* window, fractional-authorship-adjusted totals were 969 papers for Google DeepMind, 64 for Meta, 64 for OpenAI, and 62 for Anthropic. These are totals for a defined generative-AI corpus—not each lab’s complete output, annual counts, or evidence of a continuous decline since 2018. The authors supplemented OpenAlex with OpenAI and Anthropic website publications and warn that Meta may be undercounted. Their annual plot identifies DeepMind’s especially large 2023–2024 fall; it does **not** establish that all four companies followed the same trajectory. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008)

Other measures capture different phenomena. In Stanford’s *2025 AI Index*, industry-only papers among the **100 most-cited AI publications** numbered 17 in 2021, 19 in 2022, and 7 in 2023; that is a decline in this highly cited subset, **not** a count of all industry papers. Conversely, industry originated **55 notable models, or 90.2% of the notable-model set, in 2024**. Academia produced **84.9% of AI publications globally in 2023**. Taken together, these findings show a divergence between who publishes most papers and who develops most notable models; they do not justify saying that industry research or its total publication output fell throughout 2018–2026. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000059)

## How release practices diverged

| Lab | Documented progression | What the progression means |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI** | GPT-2’s full 1.5-billion-parameter model was initially withheld in 2019 and released after smaller models—a staged release. The 2020 GPT-3 paper described a 175-billion-parameter model and its training and evaluation, but the frontier model was not released as downloadable weights. In 2023, the GPT-4 *technical report* expressly omitted model size, architecture details, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, and fuller training methods, citing competition and safety. By the 2025 Transparency Index, its assessed flagship **o3** was an API release. OpenAI also released the separate, smaller **gpt-oss** open-weight models in 2025: its policy was not uniformly closed. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000051) | Publication, API availability, and weight release became distinct decisions. GPT-4 demonstrates that even a substantial public report can withhold information needed to reconstruct training. (pqac-00000041) |
| **Google / Google DeepMind** | Google’s BERT paper, first circulated in 2018, explicitly linked **code and pretrained models**. DeepMind’s 2021 AlphaFold paper made **source code, trained weights, and an inference script** available. Google DeepMind’s 2024 Gemma report released **2B and 7B pretrained and instruction-tuned checkpoints plus open-source inference/serving code**, while its later assessed flagship **Gemini 2.5** was API-accessed. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033) | This is a mixed portfolio, not abandonment of open scientific artifacts: accessible models and code coexist with a closed-weight flagship and the measured 2023–2024 publication decline. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033) |
| **Meta** | The first LLaMA models were described in a 2023 paper but distributed initially to approved researchers under a non-commercial research arrangement. **Llama 2** followed in 2023 with pretrained and chat-tuned releases under conditions permitting commercial use. In 2024 Meta publicly released pretrained and post-trained **Llama 3.1 405B** weights under its Community License, while saying multimodal extensions were *not yet* broadly released. The 2025 Index classified **Llama 4** as open-weight. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000033) | Access widened substantially relative to the initial gate, but release remained selective and licensed. A comparative openness assessment lists Llama 4’s weights as public under restrictions while its training data and training code remained private. (pqac-00000038) |
| **Anthropic** | Anthropic publicly described its **Constitutional AI** training method in a 2022 paper. Yet the **Claude 4** flagship assessed in the 2025 Index was an **API** release, not a public-weight release. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) | Publishing alignment methods and describing a deployed model do not grant researchers its trained parameters or full training pipeline. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) |

Here, *code release* means software is shared; *open weights* means trained parameters can be downloaded and examined or run subject to their license; *full training reproducibility* also requires such inputs as training data, preprocessing, training code and compute information. An API permits experiments on model behavior, but not inspection or local rerunning of its parameters. Neither a paper nor an open-weight download, on its own, establishes that the original training run can be reproduced. The distinction matters particularly for Llama and Gemma: a comparative assessment found publicly available inference code and restricted-license weights for Llama 4 and Gemma 3, but private training data and training code for both. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000038)

## What the Foundation Model Transparency Index measures

The **Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI)** measures disclosed information about companies and their selected flagship models across upstream development, model properties and downstream deployment; it is **not a publication-count index or a simple open-weights ranking**. Its reported mean score was **37/100 in 2023, 58/100 in 2024, and 40.69/100 in 2025**. For the four companies, the directly reported **2024 → 2025** scores were **Anthropic 51 → 46; Google 47 → 41; Meta 60 → 31; and OpenAI 49 → 35**. Thus Meta and OpenAI fell sharply on this measure, while Anthropic and Google fell more modestly. Meta and OpenAI, first and second among the six firms assessed in every edition in 2023, ranked last and second-to-last among those six in 2025. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000035)

The 2025 Index scored **13 developers on 100 indicators**. Only **seven** submitted their own reports; the researchers assembled public-information reports for six others, including Anthropic. Indicators and the company sample changed, some scoring standards became stricter, and the 2024 and 2025 reporting arrangements differed. Consequently, the change in the *overall mean* is not a like-for-like estimate of how much every firm reduced disclosure; individual changes are informative but also need those methodological qualifications. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035)

The Index pinpoints why a model announcement can be scientifically thin: its 2025 **training-data-properties** indicators averaged just **15%**, with eight companies scoring zero on that subdomain. Training compute and post-deployment usage and impact were also poorly disclosed. Developers often reported capability and risk evaluations without enough methods for external reproduction, and the Index found inadequate disclosure of overlap between training material and evaluation sets. Its stricter 2025 reproducibility criterion required shared evaluation **code and prompts**. These are information deficits even when a lab publishes a system card or offers model access. (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034)

## Consequences for academic research and reproducibility

Restricted weights and undisclosed data limit the questions an outside laboratory can answer. Researchers can test a permitted API’s outputs, but cannot directly inspect its parameters, independently fine-tune or rerun it locally, reconstruct its data selection, or fully check benchmark contamination and training claims. Access and compute also affect participation: an observational study of **104,226 scientific papers from 2018–2025** associated industry cloud credits with greater reliance on closed/API models, whereas public funding was associated with greater open-weight use. The study does **not** establish that credits *caused* the difference; it instead documents an access-and-control divide that can persist even when academic authors publish their own code. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000034)

There is an important countertrend. An analysis of **56,800 papers** at five AI conferences found that the share documenting **both open code and open datasets** rose from **11% in 2014 to 64% in 2024**; open-code reporting alone rose from 13% to 69%. Its estimated rise in reproducibility from 28% to 64% was **inferred from documentation and earlier replication rates, not established by rerunning every paper**. The study also found no systematic academia-versus-industry documentation advantage across its comparisons. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is **improving openness for published conference experiments alongside persistent—and in some flagship cases worsening—opacity of the most consequential proprietary systems**. Neither trend cancels the other. (pqac-00000055, pqac-00000053, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000035)

**Bottom line:** By 2026, industry disclosure had become more *layered and lab-specific*: papers, model cards, safety evaluations, API access, inference code, downloadable weights and training resources could be released separately, at different times, to different users. Evidence supports a notable 2023–2024 fall in Google DeepMind’s measured public generative-AI papers and declining FMTI scores for several flagship developers, but it also documents major open-weight and code releases and improving code/data sharing across AI conference research. A claim that *all* of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and Anthropic simply stopped publishing or opening models between 2018 and 2026 would overstate the evidence. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000035, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000055)"}

(wan2026the2025foundation pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16, wan2026the2025foundation pages 20-21)

## Consequences for academic research and reproducibility

Restricted weights and undisclosed data limit the questions an outside laboratory can answer. Researchers can test a permitted API’s outputs, but cannot directly inspect its parameters, independently fine-tune or rerun it locally, reconstruct its data selection, or fully check benchmark contamination and training claims. Access and compute also affect participation: an observational study of **104,226 scientific papers from 2018–2025** associated industry cloud credits with greater reliance on closed/API models, whereas public funding was associated with greater open-weight use. The study does **not** establish that credits *caused* the difference; it instead documents an access-and-control divide that can persist even when academic authors publish their own code. (trisovic2026openscienceclosed pages 9-10, trisovic2026openscienceclosed pages 2-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 20-21)

There is an important countertrend. An analysis of **56,800 papers** at five AI conferences found that the share documenting **both open code and open datasets** rose from **11% in 2014 to 64% in 2024**; open-code reporting alone rose from 13% to 69%. Its estimated rise in reproducibility from 28% to 64% was **inferred from documentation and earlier replication rates, not established by rerunning every paper**. The study also found no systematic academia-versus-industry documentation advantage across its comparisons. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is **improving openness for published conference experiments alongside persistent—and in some flagship cases worsening—opacity of the most consequential proprietary systems**. Neither trend cancels the other. (coakley2026theshifttoward pages 6-8, coakley2026theshifttoward pages 10-12, openai2023gpt4technicalreport pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 33-35)

# Industry AI research disclosure, 2018–2026

**The main change is selective disclosure, not a uniform end to publishing.** In the late 2010s, influential industry papers could arrive with reusable code and pretrained models, as Google’s BERT did. By the mid-2020s, leading labs still published research, but increasingly separated a paper or safety report from access to the system it described: a flagship might be available only through an API, while a different or smaller model was released with downloadable weights. Meta’s Llama family is an important counterexample to a blanket shift toward closed weights, although downloadable weights do not necessarily include training code or data. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000038, pqac-00000041)

## Publication output: what has—and has not—declined

A study of generative-AI research at selected institutions found **some broad decline in publicly available publications from 2023 to 2024, particularly at Google DeepMind**. Across its *January 2020–March 2025* window, fractional-authorship-adjusted totals were 969 papers for Google DeepMind, 64 for Meta, 64 for OpenAI, and 62 for Anthropic. These are totals for a defined generative-AI corpus—not each lab’s complete output, annual counts, or evidence of a continuous decline since 2018. The authors supplemented OpenAlex with OpenAI and Anthropic website publications and warn that Meta may be undercounted. Their annual plot identifies DeepMind’s especially large 2023–2024 fall; it does **not** establish that all four companies followed the same trajectory. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000008)

Other measures capture different phenomena. In Stanford’s *2025 AI Index*, industry-only papers among the **100 most-cited AI publications** numbered 17 in 2021, 19 in 2022, and 7 in 2023; that is a decline in this highly cited subset, **not** a count of all industry papers. Conversely, industry originated **55 notable models, or 90.2% of the notable-model set, in 2024**. Academia produced **84.9% of AI publications globally in 2023**. Taken together, these findings show a divergence between who publishes most papers and who develops most notable models; they do not justify saying that industry research or its total publication output fell throughout 2018–2026. (pqac-00000060, pqac-00000057, pqac-00000059)

## How release practices diverged

| Lab | Documented progression | What the progression means |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI** | GPT-2’s full 1.5-billion-parameter model was initially withheld in 2019 and released after smaller models—a staged release. The 2020 GPT-3 paper described a 175-billion-parameter model and its training and evaluation, but the frontier model was not released as downloadable weights. In 2023, the GPT-4 *technical report* expressly omitted model size, architecture details, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, and fuller training methods, citing competition and safety. By the 2025 Transparency Index, its assessed flagship **o3** was an API release. OpenAI also released the separate, smaller **gpt-oss** open-weight models in 2025: its policy was not uniformly closed. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000041, pqac-00000033, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000051) | Publication, API availability, and weight release became distinct decisions. GPT-4 demonstrates that even a substantial public report can withhold information needed to reconstruct training. (pqac-00000041) |
| **Google / Google DeepMind** | Google’s BERT paper, first circulated in 2018, explicitly linked **code and pretrained models**. DeepMind’s 2021 AlphaFold paper made **source code, trained weights, and an inference script** available. Google DeepMind’s 2024 Gemma report released **2B and 7B pretrained and instruction-tuned checkpoints plus open-source inference/serving code**, while its later assessed flagship **Gemini 2.5** was API-accessed. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000046, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000033) | This is a mixed portfolio, not abandonment of open scientific artifacts: accessible models and code coexist with a closed-weight flagship and the measured 2023–2024 publication decline. (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033) |
| **Meta** | The first LLaMA models were described in a 2023 paper but distributed initially to approved researchers under a non-commercial research arrangement. **Llama 2** followed in 2023 with pretrained and chat-tuned releases under conditions permitting commercial use. In 2024 Meta publicly released pretrained and post-trained **Llama 3.1 405B** weights under its Community License, while saying multimodal extensions were *not yet* broadly released. The 2025 Index classified **Llama 4** as open-weight. (pqac-00000023, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000040, pqac-00000033) | Access widened substantially relative to the initial gate, but release remained selective and licensed. A comparative openness assessment lists Llama 4’s weights as public under restrictions while its training data and training code remained private. (pqac-00000038) |
| **Anthropic** | Anthropic publicly described its **Constitutional AI** training method in a 2022 paper. Yet the **Claude 4** flagship assessed in the 2025 Index was an **API** release, not a public-weight release. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) | Publishing alignment methods and describing a deployed model do not grant researchers its trained parameters or full training pipeline. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000033) |

Here, *code release* means software is shared; *open weights* means trained parameters can be downloaded and examined or run subject to their license; *full training reproducibility* also requires such inputs as training data, preprocessing, training code and compute information. An API permits experiments on model behavior, but not inspection or local rerunning of its parameters. Neither a paper nor an open-weight download, on its own, establishes that the original training run can be reproduced. The distinction matters particularly for Llama and Gemma: a comparative assessment found publicly available inference code and restricted-license weights for Llama 4 and Gemma 3, but private training data and training code for both. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000038)

For the four companies, the directly reported **2024 → 2025** scores were **Anthropic 51 → 46; Google 47 → 41; Meta 60 → 31; and OpenAI 49 → 35**. Thus Meta and OpenAI fell sharply on this measure, while Anthropic and Google fell more modestly. Meta and OpenAI, first and second among the six firms assessed in every edition in 2023, ranked last and second-to-last among those six in 2025. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000035)

The 2025 Index scored **13 developers on 100 indicators**. Only **seven** submitted their own reports; the researchers assembled public-information reports for six others, including Anthropic. Indicators and the company sample changed, some scoring standards became stricter, and the 2024 and 2025 reporting arrangements differed. snippets: GPT-3 [30], with 175 billion parameters trained on hundreds of billions of tokens, marked the arrival of few-shot in-context learning as an emergent property of scale.

Subsequent years witnessed rapid iteration: Codex [3] applied the paradigm to code; InstructGPT [13] introduced RLHF to align model behaviour with human preferences; and ChatGPT's public release in November 2022 brought LLMs to mainstream awareness.
The period 2023–2026 has been characterised by the proliferation of model families, the open-sourcing of capable weights (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek), and the development of specialised reasoning models.
OpenAI's Generative Pre-trained Transformer series represents the most commercially influential line of LLMs to date.
GPT-1 [28] established the viability of unsupervised pre-training followed by fine-tuning.
GPT-2 [29] demonstrated emergent text generation quality that prompted concerns about misuse.
GPT-3 [30] introduced few-shot in-context learning at scale.
GPT-4 [2] achieved human-level performance on a suite of professional exams and introduced vision capabilities.
Anthropic's Constitutional AI (CAI) [36] augments RLHF with a self-critique loop guided by an explicit set of principles, reducing dependence on human labour in the preference phase.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides comparative context for the requested primary-document statements about openness, release practices, and reproducibility. It says that OpenAI’s February 2019 GPT-2 announcement withheld substantial information and did not initially release the complete 1.5-billion-parameter model. By contrast, Meta released the Llama family in 2023, but imposed use restrictions, so the models do not satisfy strict open-source criteria. The excerpt distinguishes open weights from fully open-source systems: open-weight models provide downloadable snapshots of particular versions with frozen weights, whereas full openness would include source code, training data, weights, and other parts of the production workflow. It emphasizes that access to weights can support replication, but proprietary models may change or become inaccessible. As an example of a fully open release, EleutherAI’s Pythia suite included publicly available training code, the 825 GiB Pile corpus, and checkpoints at different training stages, allowing researchers to inspect outputs and study causal interventions in training. The passage also notes that the Pile is no longer directly downloadable because of copyright issues, with the Common Pile offered as a newer alternative. These points are relevant to questions about code, weights/checkpoints, access restrictions, training data, and staged releases, but the excerpt does not cover BERT, GPT-3, AlphaFold 2, Gemma, or Constitutional AI directly.

contexts.context: The excerpt supports methodological and sampling caveats for interpreting the requested 2023–2025 scores, but it does not provide the exact individual scores for Anthropic, Google, Meta, or OpenAI, nor the overall scores (37, 58, and 40), the total number of indicators, or detailed company-by-company evidence on training datasets, compute, evaluations, code, or model weights. For 2025, the Index contacted 23 developers, compared with 19 in 2024; seven submitted transparency reports, all returning participants (AI21 Labs, Amazon, Google, IBM, Meta, OpenAI, and Writer). To maintain coverage, the researchers independently evaluated six non-submitters: xAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Alibaba, Midjourney, and Mistral, producing a total sample of 13 developers. Ten contacted companies did not participate, including several that declined or did not respond. The questionnaire was changed by raising disclosure standards, codifying external reproducibility as requiring open-source code and prompts, adding code requirements for reproducing development processes, allowing disclosures of unavailable information and contractual restrictions, focusing on top-ranked data sources, modernizing topics such as synthetic data and agent protocols, and adding organization-level indicators. These changes mean scores across editions should not be treated as perfectly comparable.

Data access and documentation are described as essential for “reproducible research.” Release transparency averages 69%, but varies widely (IBM 93%, Midjourney 16%, Grok 17%). Meta discloses training-data size and emissions (1,999 tons CO2eq), whereas OpenAI scores 10% or below on data acquisition and provides limited upstream transparency.
contexts.question: How have industry AI labs' publication, code-release and model-weight release practices changed between 2018 and 2026? Include evidence on declining or increasing publication by companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and Anthropic, staged or gated releases, the Foundation Model Transparency Index, and effects on academic research and reproducibility.

contexts.context: The excerpt offers no direct 2018–2026 publication-count trend, but the 2025 FMTI shows declining voluntary transparency participation: 7 of 23 contacted companies submitted reports, versus 14 of 19 in 2024. It evaluated Anthropic, Google, Meta, and OpenAI despite nonparticipation/participation differences; their flagship access was gated API for Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, but open weights for Meta. FMTI now requires open-sourced code and prompts for reproducible evaluations and asks for code enabling third-party training-data processing, strengthening academic reproducibility. Its stricter standards expose disclosure gaps, while API-only or staged access can constrain independent research and replication.

contexts.context: The excerpt directly documents GPT-4’s limited disclosure policy. It identifies GPT-4 at a high level as a Transformer-style model trained to predict the next token, using publicly available and third-party-licensed data, followed by fine-tuning with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). However, the report explicitly withholds architecture details—including model size—as well as hardware, training compute, dataset construction, and fuller training-method information. The stated reasons are both the competitive landscape and the safety implications of large-scale models. OpenAI says that additional technical details may be shared with selected third parties to help balance competitive and safety concerns against the scientific value of transparency. The excerpt also describes GPT-4 as multimodal, accepting image and text inputs and producing text outputs, while noting limitations such as hallucinations, a limited context window, and lack of learning from experience. It does not contain the requested comparison material for the GPT-3 paper, Meta’s Llama 2/3 reports, 2025 gpt-oss evidence, or Anthropic’s Claude flagship API; those sources would be needed to substantiate claims about detailed dataset or architecture disclosures, open-weight releases, or API-only availability.

snippets: Given both the competitive landscape and the safety implications of large-scale models like GPT-4, this report contains no further details about the architecture (including model size), hardware, training compute, dataset construction, training method, or similar.
GPT-4 is a Transformer-style model [39] pre-trained to predict the next token in a document, using both publicly available data (such as internet data) and data licensed from third-party providers.
The model was then fine-tuned using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [40].

We plan to make further technical details available to additional third parties who can advise us on how to weigh the competitive and safety considerations above against the scientific value of further transparency.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides evidence relevant to the Meta Llama 3 portion of the comparison, but it does not contain the requested OpenAI GPT-4 Technical Report quotations, GPT-3 paper details, 2025 GPT-OSS evidence, or Anthropic Claude flagship API information. For Llama 3, the report states that the largest model is a dense Transformer with 405 billion parameters and a context window of up to 128K tokens. It describes pre-training on approximately 15 trillion multilingual tokens, with a more specific figure of 15.6 trillion text tokens for the 405B flagship model, and reports training compute of 3.8 × 10^25 FLOPs—almost 50 times the largest Llama 2 model. The authors explain that they selected a standard dense Transformer rather than a mixture-of-experts architecture to improve training stability, and used supervised fine-tuning, rejection sampling, and direct preference optimization for post-training. The report says Llama 3 supports multilinguality, coding, reasoning, and tool use. Meta publicly released all three Llama 3 models under an updated Community License, including pre-trained and post-trained versions of the 405B model, while multimodal image, video, and speech extensions remained under development and were not yet released.

contexts.context: Meta’s 2023 Llama 2 paper documents an unusually open release: pretrained and fine-tuned chat models spanning 7B–70B parameters, with detailed pretraining, fine-tuning, safety, evaluation, limitations, and a “Responsible Release Strategy.” It says public models such as BLOOM, LLaMA-1, and Falcon could match closed competitors, but none then substituted for product systems like ChatGPT, Bard, or Claude. Llama 2-Chat was presented as a community-building release, enabling others to “build on our work,” while high computational requirements still concentrated development among a few players.

contexts.context: The excerpt’s 2025–26 model table shows sharply divergent disclosure. Google Gemma 3 and Meta Llama 4 publicly release inference code, hardware information, and weights, but keep training data/code and operational metadata private; weights carry restricted licenses. Nvidia Nemotron 4-340B is more permissive, while xAI’s Grok 1 is public/permissive but Grok 4.1 is entirely private. OpenAI’s o4-mini discloses none of the listed categories. The excerpt cites technical reports and model repositories, but provides no direct publication counts, Foundation Model Transparency Index scores, or evidence about 2018–26 trends, staged releases, or academic reproducibility.

contexts.context: OpenAI’s 2023 GPT-4 report illustrates increasingly restricted industry disclosure. Although it reports capabilities, safety testing, and predictable scaling—performance predicted from models using “1/1,000th” the compute—it withholds architecture, model size, hardware, compute, dataset construction, and training details, citing competition and safety. OpenAI says further details may go only to additional third parties after weighing “competitive and safety considerations” against scientific value. The report therefore documents a technical publication without releasing code or model weights, limiting independent replication and academic study; it provides no evidence here about Google DeepMind, Meta, Anthropic, or the Foundation Model Transparency Index.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides comparative openness information for several 2025-era models, but it does not contain evidence about the 2019 GPT-2 staged release, its release sizes or dates, or a GPT-2 safety assessment. It also does not discuss Meta’s initial 2023 LLaMA gated research weights, Llama 2’s 2023 commercial license, or the requested chronology across Llama 3 and Llama 4 beyond the table’s Llama 4 entry. For Llama 4, the table indicates private training data and training code, disclosed training hardware, public inference code under a permissive license, public inference hardware, public model weights under a restricted license, and private operational metadata. The excerpt likewise does not mention 2025 OpenAI gpt-oss, its 20B or 120B open weights, or their license. It does show OpenAI o4-mini as entirely private across training data, training code, hardware, inference code and hardware, model weights, and metadata. The references identify Claude 4 as an Anthropic release dated May 22, 2025, and cite Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro documentation and a 2025 technical report. Gemma 3 is cited through Google’s Hugging Face release and technical report; the table classifies its weights as public under a restricted license, with public permissively licensed inference code and hardware.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides measured evidence about reproducibility documentation and academia–industry differences in AI research from 2014–2024, but it does not directly establish causal effects of limited industry model access, API-only or private-cloud research, funding constraints, auditability, or independent external access. Across seven reproducibility variables, five conferences, and 11 years, academic papers documented more variables 177 times, industry-affiliated papers 200 times, and one comparison was tied; a binomial test found this consistent with chance rather than a systematic academia–industry difference. The authors note that industry researchers may withhold code or data because of intellectual-property protection or employer restrictions, but their aggregate results instead indicate a shift toward increased open-code and open-dataset sharing by industry-affiliated authors beginning in 2018. Regarding reproducibility practices overall, only 15 of 35 conference-variable comparisons had higher post-checklist improvement slopes, also consistent with chance (p = 0.84), so checklists did not systematically accelerate documentation. Hardware specification was the notable exception, improving after checklist adoption, particularly at NeurIPS. Thus, this excerpt supports positive documentation and code/data-sharing trends, while offering no direct empirical estimate of how restricted access to flagship industry models affects academic research, auditability, or reproducibility.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports an observational study of 104,226 papers published from 2018–2025 examining how funding and compute-access mechanisms shape academic AI research. It distinguishes non-credit infrastructure allocations, such as donated GPUs or HPC time, from vendor-specific credits and API access. Public funding is associated with broader AI engagement and greater open-weight use, while credit-based provision is associated with lower open-weight use and greater engagement with closed, larger models; the latter association is partly attributable to model scale and may reflect recipient model choice rather than an independent causal effect of credits. Non-credit allocations are associated with both model extension and openness. The authors argue that API-only access can expand participation while leaving researchers dependent on infrastructure they cannot inspect, reproduce, or run locally, creating an auditability and reproducibility concern. They recommend pairing credits with open-weight access or compute-only allocations, disclosing compute and proprietary-model access, and measuring open-weight versus API-only engagement separately. The evidence is cross-sectional, funding is not randomly assigned, acknowledgments are incomplete, and credit findings primarily describe acknowledged use. contexts.context: The excerpt from the Stanford AI Index Report 2025 (Chapter 1, Research and Development, pp. 45–46) provides statistics for notable AI model releases, not total AI publications. It states that academia led machine-learning model releases until 2014, after which industry took the lead. For 2024, Epoch AI counted 55 notable models originating from industry and none originating from academia; industry therefore accounted for 90.2% of notable AI models that year. The excerpt does not provide the corresponding 2018 industry-versus-academia notable-model totals, nor does it provide a 2018–2024 comparison of total AI publications by sector. Consequently, it cannot by itself establish whether industry publications declined uniformly over that period. The report also cautions that the Epoch AI database is manually curated, that some models may be missing, and that year-by-year counts can change as new and historic models are added. The cited source is Maslej et al., Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2025, arXiv (April 2025), DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2504.07139.
contexts.question: Find Stanford AI Index report 2025 statistics industry versus academia notable AI models in 2024 2018; compare total AI publications academia industry over 2018-2024, address misconception industry publication uniformly declining; reliable source exactly.

contexts.context: The provided Stanford AI Index 2025 excerpt supports a comparison of sectors among the 100 most-cited AI publications, not a comparison of total AI publication output from 2018 through 2024. For this top-cited subset, academia led in every reported year: 34 publications in 2021, 27 in 2022, and 42 in 2023. Industry contributed 17 in 2021, 19 in 2022, and 7 in 2023, while industry-and-academia collaborations contributed 25, 35, and 31, respectively. The report attributes the decline in industry representation partly to industrial labs publishing less frequently or disclosing fewer details as competition increased. This is evidence of a decline in industry’s share of the top-100, not proof that industry publication totals uniformly declined across all years or all publications. The excerpt does not provide the requested 2018 or 2024 sector totals, nor does it identify notable AI models from 2018 and 2024. It does identify highly cited 2023 examples—OpenAI’s GPT-4 technical report, Meta’s Llama 2 technical report, and Google’s PaLM-E—and states that the analysis uses OpenAlex citation data, supplemented by Google Scholar and Semantic Scholar. The citation-lag caveat means rankings may change in later editions.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides background on the changing balance between academic and industrial AI research, but it does not contain the requested Stanford AI Index 2025 statistics, the comparison of notable AI models in 2018 and 2024, or publication totals for academia and industry from 2018–2024. It reports that AI research expanded in both sectors while industry grew substantially faster, shifting the field’s center of gravity toward industry. In the United States, the excerpt states that the number of AI researchers rose from 6,800 in 2000 to 42,000 in 2020. Academic AI researchers increased to 12,000, while industry researchers reached 22,500. It also notes that the share of U.S. and Canadian AI PhDs entering industry rose from 21% in 2004 to nearly 70% in 2020. These claims support a broad argument about industry’s growing role, but they do not establish whether industry AI publications declined uniformly over 2018–2024; that misconception requires the specific Stanford AI Index data requested.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: How have industry AI labs' publication, code-release and model-weight release practices changed between 2018 and 2026? Include evidence on declining or increasing publication by companies such as OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and Anthropic, staged or gated releases, the Foundation Model Transparency Index, and effects on academic research and reproducibility.

# Industry AI research disclosure, 2018–2026

**The main change is selective disclosure, not a uniform end to publishing.** In the late 2010s, influential industry papers could arrive with reusable code and pretrained models, as Google’s BERT did. By the mid-2020s, leading labs still published research, but increasingly separated a paper or safety report from access to the system it described: a flagship might be available only through an API, while a different or smaller model was released with downloadable weights. Meta’s Llama family is an important counterexample to a blanket shift toward closed weights, although downloadable weights do not necessarily include training code or data. (devlin2019bertpretrainingof pages 1-2, team2024gemmaopenmodels pages 1-2, nobel2026untanglingaiopenness pages 82-83, openai2023gpt4technicalreport pages 1-3)

## Publication output: what has—and has not—declined

A study of generative-AI research at selected institutions found **some broad decline in publicly available publications from 2023 to 2024, particularly at Google DeepMind**. Across its *January 2020–March 2025* window, fractional-authorship-adjusted totals were 969 papers for Google DeepMind, 64 for Meta, 64 for OpenAI, and 62 for Anthropic. These are totals for a defined generative-AI corpus—not each lab’s complete output, annual counts, or evidence of a continuous decline since 2018. The authors supplemented OpenAlex with OpenAI and Anthropic website publications and warn that Meta may be undercounted. Their annual plot identifies DeepMind’s especially large 2023–2024 fall; it does **not** establish that all four companies followed the same trajectory. (strauss2025realworldgapsin pages 11-13, strauss2025realworldgapsin pages 31-34, strauss2025realworldgapsin pages 8-11, strauss2025realworldgapsin media cd386d58)

Other measures capture different phenomena. In Stanford’s *2025 AI Index*, industry-only papers among the **100 most-cited AI publications** numbered 17 in 2021, 19 in 2022, and 7 in 2023; that is a decline in this highly cited subset, **not** a count of all industry papers. Conversely, industry originated **55 notable models, or 90.2% of the notable-model set, in 2024**. Academia produced **84.9% of AI publications globally in 2023**. Taken together, these findings show a divergence between who publishes most papers and who develops most notable models; they do not justify saying that industry research or its total publication output fell throughout 2018–2026. (maslej2025artificialintelligenceindex pages 39-41, maslej2025artificialintelligenceindex pages 47-48, maslej2025artificialintelligenceindex pages 35-39)

## How release practices diverged

| Lab | Documented progression | What the progression means |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI** | GPT-2’s full 1.5-billion-parameter model was initially withheld in 2019 and released after smaller models—a staged release. The 2020 GPT-3 paper described a 175-billion-parameter model and its training and evaluation, but the frontier model was not released as downloadable weights. In 2023, the GPT-4 *technical report* expressly omitted model size, architecture details, hardware, training compute, dataset construction, and fuller training methods, citing competition and safety. By the 2025 Transparency Index, its assessed flagship **o3** was an API release. OpenAI also released the separate, smaller **gpt-oss** open-weight models in 2025: its policy was not uniformly closed. (stoltz2026selectinglanguagemodels pages 5-6, radfordUnknownyearlanguagemodelsare pages 1-2, brown2020languagemodelsare pages 9-11, openai2023gpt4technicalreport pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16, nobel2026untanglingaiopenness pages 82-83, trisovic2026openscienceclosed pages 2-3) | Publication, API availability, and weight release became distinct decisions. GPT-4 demonstrates that even a substantial public report can withhold information needed to reconstruct training. (openai2023gpt4technicalreport pages 1-3) |
| **Google / Google DeepMind** | Google’s BERT paper, first circulated in 2018, explicitly linked **code and pretrained models**. DeepMind’s 2021 AlphaFold paper made **source code, trained weights, and an inference script** available. Google DeepMind’s 2024 Gemma report released **2B and 7B pretrained and instruction-tuned checkpoints plus open-source inference/serving code**, while its later assessed flagship **Gemini 2.5** was API-accessed. (devlin2019bertpretrainingof pages 1-2, jumper2021highlyaccurateprotein pages 8-9, team2024gemmaopenmodels pages 1-2, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16) | This is a mixed portfolio, not abandonment of open scientific artifacts: accessible models and code coexist with a closed-weight flagship and the measured 2023–2024 publication decline. (strauss2025realworldgapsin pages 11-13, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16) |
| **Meta** | The first LLaMA models were described in a 2023 paper but distributed initially to approved researchers under a non-commercial research arrangement. **Llama 2** followed in 2023 with pretrained and chat-tuned releases under conditions permitting commercial use. In 2024 Meta publicly released pretrained and post-trained **Llama 3.1 405B** weights under its Community License, while saying multimodal extensions were *not yet* broadly released. The 2025 Index classified **Llama 4** as open-weight. (touvron2023llamaopenand pages 1-2, singh2025tracingtheevolution pages 28-29, touvron2023llama2open pages 1-3, grattafiori2024thellama3 pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16) | Access widened substantially relative to the initial gate, but release remained selective and licensed. A comparative openness assessment lists Llama 4’s weights as public under restrictions while its training data and training code remained private. (nobel2026untanglingaiopenness pages 82-83) |
| **Anthropic** | Anthropic publicly described its **Constitutional AI** training method in a 2022 paper. Yet the **Claude 4** flagship assessed in the 2025 Index was an **API** release, not a public-weight release. (bai2212constitutionalaiharmlessness pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16) | Publishing alignment methods and describing a deployed model do not grant researchers its trained parameters or full training pipeline. (bai2212constitutionalaiharmlessness pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16) |

Here, *code release* means software is shared; *open weights* means trained parameters can be downloaded and examined or run subject to their license; *full training reproducibility* also requires such inputs as training data, preprocessing, training code and compute information. An API permits experiments on model behavior, but not inspection or local rerunning of its parameters. Neither a paper nor an open-weight download, on its own, establishes that the original training run can be reproduced. The distinction matters particularly for Llama and Gemma: a comparative assessment found publicly available inference code and restricted-license weights for Llama 4 and Gemma 3, but private training data and training code for both. (stoltz2026selectinglanguagemodels pages 6-8, nobel2026untanglingaiopenness pages 82-83)

## What the Foundation Model Transparency Index measures

The **Foundation Model Transparency Index (FMTI)** measures disclosed information about companies and their selected flagship models across upstream development, model properties and downstream deployment; it is **not a publication-count index or a simple open-weights ranking**. Its reported mean score was **37/100 in 2023, 58/100 in 2024, and 40.69/100 in 2025**. For the four companies, the directly reported **2024 → 2025** scores were **Anthropic 51 → 46; Google 47 → 41; Meta 60 → 31; and OpenAI 49 → 35**. Thus Meta and OpenAI fell sharply on this measure, while Anthropic and Google fell more modestly. Meta and OpenAI, first and second among the six firms assessed in every edition in 2023, ranked last and second-to-last among those six in 2025. (wan2026the2025foundation pages 3-4, wan2026the2025foundation pages 33-35)

The 2025 Index scored **13 developers on 100 indicators**. Only **seven** submitted their own reports; the researchers assembled public-information reports for six others, including Anthropic. Indicators and the company sample changed, some scoring standards became stricter, and the 2024 and 2025 reporting arrangements differed. Consequently, the change in the *overall mean* is not a like-for-like estimate of how much every firm reduced disclosure; individual changes are informative but also need those methodological qualifications. (wan2026the2025foundation pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16, wan2026the2025foundation pages 33-35)

The Index pinpoints why a model announcement can be scientifically thin: its 2025 **training-data-properties** indicators averaged just **15%**, with eight companies scoring zero on that subdomain. Training compute and post-deployment usage and impact were also poorly disclosed. Developers often reported capability and risk evaluations without enough methods for external reproduction, and the Index found inadequate disclosure of overlap between training material and evaluation sets. Its stricter 2025 reproducibility criterion required shared evaluation **code and prompts**. These are information deficits even when a lab publishes a system card or offers model access. (wan2026the2025foundation pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 14-16, wan2026the2025foundation pages 20-21)

## Consequences for academic research and reproducibility

Restricted weights and undisclosed data limit the questions an outside laboratory can answer. Researchers can test a permitted API’s outputs, but cannot directly inspect its parameters, independently fine-tune or rerun it locally, reconstruct its data selection, or fully check benchmark contamination and training claims. Access and compute also affect participation: an observational study of **104,226 scientific papers from 2018–2025** associated industry cloud credits with greater reliance on closed/API models, whereas public funding was associated with greater open-weight use. The study does **not** establish that credits *caused* the difference; it instead documents an access-and-control divide that can persist even when academic authors publish their own code. (trisovic2026openscienceclosed pages 9-10, trisovic2026openscienceclosed pages 2-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 20-21)

There is an important countertrend. An analysis of **56,800 papers** at five AI conferences found that the share documenting **both open code and open datasets** rose from **11% in 2014 to 64% in 2024**; open-code reporting alone rose from 13% to 69%. Its estimated rise in reproducibility from 28% to 64% was **inferred from documentation and earlier replication rates, not established by rerunning every paper**. The study also found no systematic academia-versus-industry documentation advantage across its comparisons. Therefore, the best-supported conclusion is **improving openness for published conference experiments alongside persistent—and in some flagship cases worsening—opacity of the most consequential proprietary systems**. Neither trend cancels the other. (coakley2026theshifttoward pages 6-8, coakley2026theshifttoward pages 10-12, openai2023gpt4technicalreport pages 1-3, wan2026the2025foundation pages 33-35)

**Bottom line:** By 2026, industry disclosure had become more *layered and lab-specific*: papers, model cards, safety evaluations, API access, inference code, downloadable weights and training resources could be released separately, at different times, to different users. Evidence supports a notable 2023–2024 fall in Google DeepMind’s measured public generative-AI papers and declining FMTI scores for several flagship developers, but it also documents major open-weight and code releases and improving code/data sharing across AI conference research. A claim that *all* of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Meta and Anthropic simply stopped publishing or opening models between 2018 and 2026 would overstate the evidence. (strauss2025realworldgapsin pages 11-13, team2024gemmaopenmodels pages 1-2, wan2026the2025foundation pages 33-35, grattafiori2024thellama3 pages 1-3, coakley2026theshifttoward pages 6-8)
